title: Math for ML: Quick Revision Notes
summary: Night-before revision of the math behind machine learning: vectors and matrices, derivatives and the chain rule, gradients and gradient descent, probability, Bayes' rule, expectation and variance, and loss functions.

chapters.title: Vectors, Dot Products and Matrices
points: A vector is an ordered list of numbers (a point or direction in n-D space); a matrix is a 2-D grid of shape (rows, cols)
Dot product a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ = |a||b|cosθ: zero means orthogonal, large positive means same direction
Cosine similarity = a·b / (|a||b|) ignores length and is bounded in [-1, 1]; the dot product scales with magnitude
Matrix product (m×n)(n×p) = (m×p): inner dimensions must match, and AB ≠ BA in general
Common mistake: confusing element-wise multiply (*) with matrix multiply (@), and forgetting that (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ

chapters.title: Derivatives and the Chain Rule
points: Derivative f'(x) is the instantaneous rate of change, i.e. the slope of the tangent line at x
Rules to memorise: (xⁿ)' = nxⁿ⁻¹, (eˣ)' = eˣ, (ln x)' = 1/x, sum rule, product rule (uv)' = u'v + uv'
Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))·g'(x); multiply local derivatives along the path
Example: sigmoid σ(x) = 1/(1+e⁻ˣ) has σ' = σ(1-σ), at most 0.25, so many stacked layers make gradients vanish
Common mistake: dropping the inner derivative g'(x), or forgetting that backprop is the chain rule applied layer by layer

chapters.title: Gradients and Gradient Descent
points: Gradient ∇f is the vector of partial derivatives; it points in the direction of steepest increase, so you step against it
Update rule: θ ← θ − η∇L(θ), where η is the learning rate
Batch uses all data per step (stable, slow); SGD uses one sample (noisy, fast); mini-batch uses 32–256 samples and is the default
Example: L = (w−3)², gradient 2(w−3); with w=0 and η=0.1, w moves to 0.6 after one step
Common mistakes: η too large diverges, η too small crawls; unscaled features create elongated valleys; gradient 0 can be a saddle point or local minimum, not necessarily the global one

chapters.title: Probability, Bayes' Rule, Expectation and Variance
points: Probabilities lie in [0,1] and sum to 1 over all outcomes; P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B); independent events satisfy P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B)
Bayes' rule: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B), i.e. posterior ∝ likelihood × prior
Example: a test with 99% sensitivity and 1% false positive rate for a disease with 1% prevalence gives P(disease|positive) ≈ 50%
Expectation E[X] = Σ x·P(x) is linear: E[aX+bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]; variance Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])², std = √Var
Common mistake: confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A) (base rate neglect), and assuming Var(X+Y) = Var(X)+Var(Y) when X and Y are not independent

chapters.title: Loss Functions
points: A loss function measures prediction error as one scalar that gradient descent minimises
MSE = mean((y−ŷ)²) is for regression; it is smooth but punishes outliers heavily, while MAE is robust to outliers but has a non-smooth gradient at 0
Binary cross-entropy = −[y·log p + (1−y)·log(1−p)]; categorical cross-entropy = −Σ yᵢ log pᵢ over softmax outputs
Example: true class probability 0.9 gives loss ≈ 0.105, while 0.1 gives ≈ 2.30, so confident wrong predictions are penalised heavily
Common mistakes: using MSE for classification, applying softmax twice when the loss already includes it, and taking log(0) without clipping

chapters.title: Math for ML Cheat Sheet
points: Dot product a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ; cosine = a·b/(|a||b|); matrix shapes (m×n)(n×p)=(m×p)
Chain rule: multiply local derivatives; sigmoid' = σ(1−σ); (xⁿ)' = nxⁿ⁻¹
Gradient descent: θ ← θ − η∇L; mini-batch is the default; tune η first
Bayes: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence; Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])²
Loss choice: MSE for regression, cross-entropy for classification; always clip before log
